quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on what a job is, how its costs are classified and the three costing systems.

questions.q: In job costing, costs are assigned to
options: All units produced in a month, averaged
A distinct unit, batch or lot of a product or service
questions.explain: A job is a distinct product or service — a printing lot, a house — and its costs are collected separately. Averaging over all units is process costing.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a job?
options: Spinning Ne 20/1 yarn continuously for stock
Printing a particular design on 10,000 m of a customer's fabric
Generating steam for the whole mill
questions.explain: A custom lot made for a specific customer is a job; continuous production of identical yarn is costed by process costing.

questions.q: In the printing job, which cost is a direct cost of the job?
questions.explain: Fabric and colours and chemicals are consumed by this job and traced to it; utilities, depreciation and other overhead are indirect-cost pools allocated through a rate.

questions.q: An indirect-cost pool is
options: A direct cost that is too small to trace
A grouping of indirect costs, such as utilities or overhead, to be allocated
The total cost of one job
The customer's budget for the job
questions.explain: The lecture's two pools are monthly utilities (Rs 3,000,000) and overhead (Rs 10,000,000); each pool is allocated to jobs via a cost-allocation base.

questions.q: The cost-allocation base chosen in the lecture's printing example is
questions.explain: Indirect costs are spread over monthly production in metres, giving a rate per metre that is multiplied by the job's metres.

questions.q: Under normal costing, direct costs are traced in the same way as under actual costing.
questions.explain: Normal costing changes only the indirect-cost rate (budgeted instead of actual); direct costs such as fabric and colours are still traced at actual amounts.

questions.q: Budgeted costing differs from normal costing in that
options: Budgeted rates are used even for direct costs
Actual rates are used for everything
Jobs are costed only at year end
questions.explain: Normal costing budgets only the indirect rate; budgeted costing extends budgeted rates to direct costs as well.

questions.q: The main drawback of actual costing is that
options: A job cannot be costed until the period ends and actual indirect costs are known
questions.explain: Actual costing waits until the end of the period for the exact indirect costs; normal costing exists so a job can be costed the day it finishes.

questions.q: A favourable variance means the actual rate was higher than the standard rate.
questions.explain: A favourable variance arises when actual cost is below standard; the lecture reads it as the department operating efficiently, while an unfavourable one alerts management.

questions.q: The six steps of job costing begin with
options: Developing the rate per unit of base
questions.explain: Identify the job, then its direct costs, the indirect-cost pools, the allocation base, the rate, and finally assign the costs.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The allocation-rate arithmetic and how the job cost moves when the inputs move.

questions.q: The indirect cost rate per metre is
options: Total indirect pools ÷ total monthly production in metres
questions.explain: (3,000,000 + 10,000,000) ÷ monthly production = Rs 20 per metre. Dividing by the job size alone would load the whole month's overhead onto one job.

questions.q: The indirect cost allocated to a job equals
options: Rate per metre × job size in metres
questions.explain: Rs 20 × 10,000 m = Rs 200,000 for the printing lot.

questions.q: Total cost of the job is
options: Fabric + dyes and chemicals + allocated indirect cost
questions.explain: Direct costs (1,100,000 + 120,000) plus the allocated 200,000 = Rs 1,420,000. Adding the whole monthly overhead is a common error.

questions.q: If total monthly production rises while the indirect-cost pools stay the same, the rate per metre
questions.explain: The same pool is spread over more metres, so each metre carries less; a job finished in a busy month looks cheaper under actual costing.

questions.q: Cost per metre of printed fabric = total cost of the job ÷ job size in metres.
questions.explain: Rs 1,420,000 ÷ 10,000 m = Rs 142 per metre in the lecture sheet.

questions.q: If the overhead pool grows by Rs 1,300,000 in a month of 650,000 m production, the rate per metre rises by
questions.explain: 1,300,000 ÷ 650,000 = Rs 2 per metre extra; the base figure of Rs 20 comes from 13,000,000 ÷ 650,000.

questions.q: Under normal costing the indirect-cost rate is
questions.explain: Both numerator and denominator come from the budget so the rate is known in advance; actual ÷ actual is actual costing.

questions.q: A job's fabric cost in rupees is
options: Grey fabric consumed × grey fabric price per metre
Grey fabric consumed ÷ price per metre
questions.explain: The sheet multiplies metres of grey fabric consumed by its price per metre; fabric consumed can differ from the job size because of shrinkage and waste.

questions.q: If a variance arises on a job processed at the standard rate, the lecture says it is applied to the job orders processed and the shop rate adjusted if necessary.
questions.explain: The variance is spread over the jobs done at that rate, and if it persists the standard (shop) rate is revised.

questions.q: Doubling the job size from 10,000 m to 20,000 m, with the same rate per metre, makes the allocated indirect cost
questions.explain: Allocation is proportional to the base: 20,000 × Rs 20 = Rs 400,000. The rate itself does not change because the pools and monthly production are the same.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the printing job cost sheet and some variations on it.

questions.q: Monthly utilities are Rs 3,000,000 and monthly overhead Rs 10,000,000; total monthly production is 650,000 m. What is the indirect cost rate per metre?
A printing job of 10,000 m is allocated indirect cost at Rs 20 per metre. How much indirect cost is assigned to the job?
Grey fabric consumed is 10,000 m at Rs 110 per metre. What is the fabric cost of the job?
Fabric Rs 1,100,000, dyes and chemicals Rs 120,000, allocated utilities and overhead Rs 200,000. Total cost of the job?
A job costing Rs 1,420,000 produced 10,000 m of printed fabric. Cost per metre?
In a slow month production fell to 500,000 m with the same pools (Rs 13,000,000). How much indirect cost is allocated to a 10,000 m job that month?
A 4,000 m job used 4,200 m of grey fabric at Rs 95 per metre, Rs 60,000 of colours, and indirect cost at Rs 20 per metre of job size. Cost per metre of printed fabric, to two decimals?
Under normal costing the budgeted pools are Rs 12,600,000 and budgeted production 700,000 m. What rate per metre is used?
questions.explain: 12,600,000 ÷ 700,000 = Rs 18 per metre, known at the start of the month.

questions.q: If the customer is charged Rs 160 per metre for the 10,000 m job costing Rs 142 per metre, the profit on the job is
questions.explain: (160 − 142) × 10,000 = Rs 180,000. Rs 18 is the profit per metre, not for the job.

questions.q: Dyes and chemicals for a job cost Rs 120,000 for 10,000 m. If a second job of 25,000 m uses colour at the same rate, its dye cost is
questions.explain: Rs 12 per metre × 25,000 m = Rs 300,000. Rs 250,000 wrongly uses Rs 10 per metre.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions in a printing or processing unit where job costing shapes the answer.

questions.q: A customer wants a quotation the day the sample lot is finished, but the month's utility bills arrive three weeks later. The costing office should use
options: Actual costing and ask the customer to wait
Normal costing with a budgeted indirect rate
questions.explain: Normal costing was designed for exactly this: direct costs at actual, indirect cost at a budgeted rate, so the job can be costed immediately.

questions.q: A print house allocates utilities on metres, but its rotary printer uses far more steam on heavy fabrics than on light ones. The likely problem is
options: Heavy-fabric jobs are undercosted and light-fabric jobs overcosted
The rate per metre is too high for everything
There is no problem; metres are always correct
questions.explain: A single metre-based rate gives every metre the same utility charge, so jobs that really consume more utilities are undercharged — a reason to choose the allocation base carefully.

questions.q: A job used 10,500 m of grey fabric to deliver 10,000 m of printed fabric. In the job cost sheet, the fabric cost should be based on
options: 10,000 m, because that is what the customer receives
10,500 m, because that is what the job consumed
questions.explain: Direct costs are the resources actually consumed by the job; the loss of 500 m is part of its cost and raises the cost per delivered metre.

questions.q: If the actual overhead for the month turns out higher than budgeted, the jobs costed under normal costing during that month were undercosted.
questions.explain: They carried the lower budgeted rate; the unfavourable variance is then applied to the job orders processed and the shop rate adjusted if necessary.

questions.q: Two jobs of 10,000 m each: Job A is a one-colour design, Job B a six-colour design needing six screens. Allocating all overhead by metres means
options: Both jobs get the same overhead, although B used more set-up effort
Job B gets six times the overhead
questions.explain: Metres are identical so the allocated indirect cost is identical; screen engraving and set-up would need a separate pool with a driver such as number of screens to be fair.

questions.q: A printing unit budgets overhead of Rs 9,000,000 and utilities Rs 2,700,000 for a month of 600,000 m. A 15,000 m job uses 15,300 m of grey fabric at Rs 120 and Rs 180,000 of colours. What is the job's total cost under normal costing?
The cost accounting department finds that colour consumption on a job ran 15 % above standard. According to the lecture, this is
options: An unfavourable variance that alerts management to possible corrective action
A change in the allocation base
questions.explain: Actual above standard is unfavourable; the lecture says such a variance signals that corrective action may be required.

questions.q: A merchandiser asks why the same 10,000 m design cost Rs 142 per metre in January and Rs 148 per metre in February under actual costing, with identical fabric and colour costs. The most likely cause is
options: February's monthly production was lower, raising the rate per metre
questions.explain: With direct costs unchanged, the extra Rs 6 per metre must come from a higher indirect rate — the same pools spread over fewer metres in February.

questions.q: A house builder, a garment exporter making a 5,000-piece custom order and a sugar refinery: which would NOT normally use job costing?
questions.explain: Sugar is a mass-produced identical product, costed by averaging (process costing); a house and a custom garment order are distinct jobs.

questions.q: A manager wants to lower the cost per metre of printed fabric without changing suppliers or prices. Which lever is available in the job cost sheet?
options: Reduce fabric and colour wastage so less is consumed per metre delivered
Increase the job size to lower the indirect rate
questions.explain: Consuming less grey fabric and colour per metre delivered cuts direct cost. A bigger job does not lower the rate per metre, and changing the costing system changes the timing, not the real cost.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder mixes across the lecture: rates, variances and the difference between the three costing systems.

questions.q: Monthly pools total Rs 13,000,000. A 10,000 m job was allocated Rs 200,000 of indirect cost. What was the total monthly production in metres?
A student computes the job's indirect cost as Rs 13,000,000 ÷ 10,000 m = Rs 1,300 per metre. The error is
options: Dividing the pools by the job size instead of by total monthly production
questions.explain: The whole month's overhead belongs to all 650,000 m produced, not to one job; the correct rate is Rs 20 per metre.

questions.q: Under normal costing the budgeted rate was Rs 20 per metre on 650,000 m. Actual pools came to Rs 13,650,000 on the same production. By how many rupees per metre was each job undercosted?
questions.explain: Actual rate = 13,650,000 ÷ 650,000 = Rs 21; the jobs carried Rs 20, so they were undercosted by Rs 1 per metre — an unfavourable variance.

questions.q: Under budgeted costing, the fabric cost on a job cost sheet would be the actual grey fabric consumed at its actual purchase price.
questions.explain: Budgeted costing applies budgeted rates even to direct costs; only actual and normal costing trace direct costs at actual amounts.

questions.q: Which statement correctly ranks the three systems by how much actual data they use, from most to least?
questions.explain: Actual costing uses actual direct and indirect costs; normal budgets only the indirect rate; budgeted costing uses budgeted rates for direct costs too.

questions.q: A job of 8,000 m has total cost Rs 1,200,000 of which Rs 160,000 is allocated indirect cost. If the indirect rate is revised upward by 10 %, what is the new cost per metre of the job?
questions.explain: Extra indirect = 16,000; new total = 1,216,000; ÷ 8,000 = Rs 152 per metre (up from Rs 150).

questions.q: A printing job sheet shows fabric Rs 1,100,000, colours Rs 120,000, indirect Rs 200,000 and cost per metre Rs 142. If the job had been only 5,000 m with the same per-metre consumption and rate, the cost per metre would be
questions.explain: Every element — fabric, colours and allocated indirect cost — scales with metres, so the cost per metre stays Rs 142; only the total halves to Rs 710,000.

questions.q: Variance analysis in the lecture compares
options: The standard rate with the actual rate
questions.explain: The cost accounting department compares standard and actual rates; the difference is the variance, favourable or unfavourable.

questions.q: Jobs totalling 200,000 m were processed at a standard indirect rate of Rs 20 per metre, but the actual rate proved to be Rs 20.75. What total variance (positive number of rupees) must be applied to those job orders?
questions.explain: 0.75 × 200,000 = Rs 150,000 unfavourable, spread over the jobs processed as the lecture describes.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches cost object and costing method?
options: A 10,000 m custom print lot — job costing; continuous Ne 20/1 yarn — process costing
A 10,000 m custom print lot — process costing; continuous Ne 20/1 yarn — job costing
questions.explain: The distinct, custom lot is a job; identical yarn produced continuously for stock is costed by averaging over all units, which is process costing (the subject of the next lecture).
